newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish PM's economic plans hit by law annulment.
newsitem.headline: Turkish PM's economic plans hit by law annulment.

text.p: Turkey's Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan faced the first major setback to his ambitious economic plans on Thursday with the court annulment of a law enabling his government to sell state property.

Erbakan's coalition government hoped to raise 300 trillion lira ($2.9 billion) from the sell-offs which are among a series of measures ultimately aimed at raising over $50 billion in the country's fight against soaring inflation and widening government budget deficits.
His grand economic vision has been met with considerable scepticism by economic analysts.
The constitutional court annulled the sell-off law, which was announced in September, after 113 deputies from two opposition left-wing parties sought its cancellation, a court official told Reuters.
The announcement sparked concern on the Istanbul Stock Exchange, where the market index slid 2.5 percent before recovering to close down 1.09 percent on the day.

Erbakan played down the annulment's significance and said the government would consider a response. He told reporters in Ankara that fresh revenues of $20 billion expected to be raised in 1997 would cushion any blow from lost sell-offs.

Since coming to power in late June, Erbakan has focused on privatisation and pushing through measures such as the property sales, leasing of power stations and issuing foreign currency debt as ways to restore stability to the country's finances.

Turkey's economy is struggling under the heavy burden of 80 percent annual inflation and a budget deficit expected to widen to 1,300 trillion lira, or 10 percent of gross domestic product, by the end of 1996.
The Islamist leader responded to the task by pledging to reduce inflation and interest rates and produce a zero-deficit budget for 1997.
Parliament is this week debating the draft budget, described by Erbakan as a "revolution" in the 73-year history of the Turkish Republic. Approval of the draft is set for December 18.

The international response to the revenue and budget plans betrays concern. U.S. ratings agency Standard & Poor's put Turkey, for which it has set a B+ rating, on CreditWatch with negative implications in July.

Japan's JCR agency downgraded Turkey to BB+ from BB in November and the International Monetary Fund has urged Turkey to make progress on a stability programme -- seen as vital if a stand-by accord is to be granted.
Financial analysts say only a significant acceleration of Turkey's stalled privatisation process would make Erbakan's revenue plans feasible.
The privatisation agency targets revenues of some $5 billion from 1997 sell-offs, though only some $3 billion has been raised since the programme's inception in 1986.

But economic analysts say that Turkey's failing credibility in international markets, its lack of domestic capital and the concentration on populist issues by leading parties all cast considerable doubt on the possibility of achieving these targets. ($=104,300 lira)
